flashcards.front: Why combine locks, badges, biometrics and mantraps?
flashcards.back_definition: Each covers a different gap, so layering them is defence in depth: no single failure exposes the protected space.
flashcards.back_example: Badge to enter the building, PIN plus fingerprint for the server room, mantrap at the data hall.
flashcards.back_confusion: Duplicating one control type adds cost without closing new gaps.

flashcards.front: Keyed lock vs RFID badge reader?
flashcards.back_definition: A keyed lock works without power but leaves no record and cannot be revoked remotely. A badge reader logs every use and can cut off a lost badge at once.
flashcards.back_example: A lost badge is disabled in the console in seconds; a lost key means changing the lock.
flashcards.back_confusion: Keep a mechanical lock as a fallback: if the badge system fails, the door should not be left open.
flashcards.back_hook: Keys remember nothing; badges remember everything.

flashcards.back_definition: A small room with two interlocked doors: the second will not open until the first has closed, so only one person passes per authorised entry.
flashcards.back_example: A data centre entrance where the inner door opens only after the outer door locks and a badge is verified.
flashcards.back_confusion: A mantrap prevents tailgating; CCTV only records it.
flashcards.back_hook: One door at a time, one person at a time.

flashcards.back_definition: False acceptance rate: how often the system lets in the wrong person. False rejection rate: how often it refuses the right person.
flashcards.back_example: Lowering the match threshold cuts FRR but raises FAR.
flashcards.back_confusion: The crossover error rate (CER), where FAR equals FRR, is used to compare systems; lower is better.
flashcards.back_hook: FAR lets the stranger in; FRR locks the owner out.

flashcards.front: Why shouldn't biometrics be the only factor?
flashcards.back_definition: No biometric is perfect (FAR is never zero), prints can be lifted and faked, and you cannot change your fingerprint after it leaks.
flashcards.back_example: Researchers have fooled fingerprint sensors with prints lifted from a glass.
flashcards.back_confusion: Use a biometric with a badge or PIN, not instead of them.
flashcards.back_hook: You can reset a password, not a thumb.

flashcards.front: Is CCTV a preventive or detective control?
flashcards.back_definition: Detective: it records and helps spot intrusions, but cannot physically stop one. Visible cameras also deter.
flashcards.back_example: Footage shows who entered the loading dock at 2 a.m.
flashcards.back_confusion: Pair cameras with preventive controls (fences, locks) and a response plan.
flashcards.back_hook: A camera watches; a lock stops.

flashcards.back_definition: Active: someone watches live feeds and can respond as it happens. Passive: video is recorded and reviewed after an incident.
flashcards.back_example: A guard sees a fence climber live and calls police: active monitoring.
flashcards.back_confusion: Passive recording is cheaper but only helps after the damage.

flashcards.front: What new risk do IP cameras bring?
flashcards.back_definition: They sit on the network, so weak passwords, old firmware or internet exposure let attackers view, disable or pivot through them.
flashcards.back_example: Botnets such as Mirai took over cameras that still used factory passwords.
flashcards.back_confusion: Put cameras on their own network segment and change default credentials.
flashcards.back_hook: A camera on the network is also a computer on the network.

flashcards.front: What is a camera blind spot, and how is it found?
flashcards.back_definition: An area no camera covers. It is found by mapping each camera's field of view against the floor plan and walking the site.
flashcards.back_example: A loading dock door just outside two cameras' views becomes the intruder's route.
flashcards.back_confusion: More cameras do not help if they all cover the same spots.
flashcards.back_hook: If no camera sees it, it didn't happen on tape.

flashcards.front: What do security guards add that technology cannot?
flashcards.back_definition: Judgment and response: they challenge strangers, spot social engineering, enforce escort rules and act when systems fail.
flashcards.back_example: A guard notices a "delivery driver" heading for the server room instead of reception.
flashcards.back_confusion: Electronics and guards cover different failure modes; removing guards removes judgment.

flashcards.front: What do visitor logs and escort policies do?
flashcards.back_definition: The log records who visited, who sponsored them and when they left; the escort rule keeps every visitor with an employee at all times.
flashcards.back_example: A contractor signs in at 10:02, is escorted to room 4, and signs out at 11:30.
flashcards.back_confusion: A visitor log is an audit and deterrent tool, not a barrier on its own.
flashcards.back_hook: Write them down, walk them around.

flashcards.front: What is hot aisle / cold aisle?
flashcards.back_definition: A rack layout where server fronts face a cold aisle of supply air and backs face a hot aisle of exhaust, so hot and cold air do not mix.
flashcards.back_example: Cold air rises through floor vents in front of the racks; hot air is drawn back to the cooling units behind.
flashcards.back_confusion: Mixing the aisles creates hot spots even when the room thermostat looks fine.
flashcards.back_hook: Faces in the cold, backs in the heat.

flashcards.front: What safe environmental ranges do data centres aim for?
flashcards.back_definition: Commonly about 18 to 27 °C at the server inlet (ASHRAE's recommended range) with controlled humidity: too dry risks static discharge, too damp risks condensation.
flashcards.back_example: An alert fires when the inlet temperature passes 27 °C.
flashcards.back_confusion: Colder is not always safer: the safe window has a lower limit too.
flashcards.back_hook: Not too hot, not too cold, not too dry, not too wet.

flashcards.back_definition: Very Early Smoke Detection Apparatus: it constantly samples air through pipes and detects tiny amounts of smoke long before a normal detector would.
flashcards.back_example: VESDA alerts on an overheating power supply before any flame appears.
flashcards.back_confusion: Detection is not suppression: VESDA warns; the clean-agent system puts the fire out.
flashcards.back_hook: Smells smoke before you see it.
